# Exercise 06 Solution {.unnumbered}

# • Solution {.unnumbered}

### Preliminaries {.unnumbered}

Load in dataset and libraries of interest...


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
library(infer)
f <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/difiore/ada-datasets/main/tbs-2006-2008-ranges.csv"
d <- read_csv(f, col_names = TRUE)
head(d)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## # A tibble: 6 × 9
##   id       sex   sex.code mcp50 mcp80 mcp95 kernel50 kernel80 kernel95
##   <chr>    <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1 Ana      F            1 123.   182.  331.     75.1     185.     330.
## 2 Andreo   M            2 136.   238.  367.    101.      232.     416.
## 3 Buka     F            1  98.2  202.  234.     60.5     161.     296.
## 4 Eva      F            1 104.   193.  352.     82.2     202.     355.
## 5 Evita    F            1 104.   183.  365.     82.6     190.     367.
## 6 Geronimo M            2 116.   286.  402.    125.      285.     502.
```

## Challenge {.unnumbered}

#### Step 1 {.unnumbered}

- Reduce the dataset to just the variables of interest.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
d <- d |> select(sex, kernel95)
head(d)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## # A tibble: 6 × 2
##   sex   kernel95
##   <chr>    <dbl>
## 1 F         330.
## 2 M         416.
## 3 F         296.
## 4 F         355.
## 5 F         367.
## 6 M         502.
```


:::
:::


#### Step 2 {.unnumbered}

- Determine the mean, standard deviation, and standard error in “kernel95” home range size for each sex.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
hr_summary <- d |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(kernel95),
    sd = sd(kernel95),
    n = n(),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )
hr_summary
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## # A tibble: 2 × 5
##   sex    mean    sd     n    se
##   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl>
## 1 F      319.  65.7    11  19.8
## 2 M      430.  58.3     9  19.4
```


:::
:::


#### Step 3 {.unnumbered}

- Create boxplots comparing “kernel95” home range size by sex.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
p <- ggplot(data = d, aes(x = sex, y = kernel95)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter()
p
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


#### Step 4 {.unnumbered}

- For each sex, generate a bootstrap distribution for mean kernel95 home range size.

> **NOTE:** The code below does this for males... simply replace "M" with "F" in the `filter()` statement to do the same for females.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# ci in mean HR size
n_boot <- 10000
s <- d |> filter(sex == "M")

# option 1 - using a loop
boot <- vector()
# the size of each bootstrap sample should equivalent to the size our original sample
for (i in 1:n_boot) {
  boot[[i]] <-
    mean(sample(s$kernel95, length(s$kernel95), replace = TRUE))
}

# option 2 - using the replicate() function
boot <- replicate(
  n_boot,
  mean(sample(s$kernel95, size = length(s$kernel95), replace = TRUE))
)

# option 3 - using {infer}
boot <- s |>
  rep_sample_n(
    replace = TRUE,
    size = nrow(s),
    reps = 10000
  ) |>
  group_by(replicate) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(kernel95)) |>
  pull(mean) # pull out mean column as vector
```
:::


#### Step 5 {.unnumbered}

- Plot the resulting bootstrap sampling distribution and plot an appropriate normal distribution over the bootstrap sampling distribution.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
se <- sd(boot)
histogram(boot)
plotDist("norm", mean(boot), se, add = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


#### Step 6 {.unnumbered}

- Calculate a 95% confidence interval around for the mean kernel95 home range size for each sex...

  - Using the `quantile()` method applied directly to your bootstrap sampling distribution, and

  - Using the theory-based "standard error" method, based on `qnorm()` and the standard deviation of your bootstrap sampling distribution.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
(ci_boot <- c(
  quantile(boot, 0.025),
  quantile(boot, 0.975)
))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
##     2.5%    97.5% 
## 395.0336 465.0215
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
(ci_theory <- mean(s$kernel95) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## [1] 394.2359 465.2455
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# or

(ci_theory <- mean(s$kernel95) + qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975)) * se)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## [1] 394.2359 465.2455
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ladd(
  panel.abline(v = ci_boot, col = "red", lty = 3, lwd = 2)
)

ladd(
  panel.abline(v = ci_theory, col = "blue", lty = 1, lwd = 2)
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


We can also do all of the above using the {infer} package's `specify()` → `generate()` → `calculate()` → `visualize()` workflow...


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# option 4 - using {infer}
boot <- s |>
  specify(response = kernel95) |>
  generate(reps = n_boot, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

ci_boot <- boot |>
  get_confidence_interval(
    type = "percentile", level = 0.95
  )

ci_theory <- boot |>
  get_confidence_interval(
    type = "se", level = 0.95,
    point_estimate = mean(s$kernel95)
  )

visualize(boot) + shade_confidence_interval(endpoints = ci_theory, color = "blue", lty = 1, fill = "#c0c0c0") + shade_confidence_interval(endpoints = ci_boot, color = "red", lty = 3, fill = "#c0c0c0")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


#### Step 7 {.unnumbered}

- Use simulation-based permutation to evaluate the difference in mean kernel95 home range size for males versus females. To do this, you will want to shuffle either the variable "sex" or "kernel95" home range size a total of 10,000 times, recalculating mean kernel95 size by sex for each permuted sample and then compare the difference in male and female kernel95 means from your original sample to the permutation distribution for the difference in means. We can do this with a `for()` loop...


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
obs_diff <- d |>
  summarize(diff = mean(kernel95[sex == "M"]) -
    mean(kernel95[sex == "F"])) |>
  pull(diff)

n_perm <- 10000 # number of permutations
# create a dummy vector to hold results for each permutation
perm_diff <- vector()
for (i in 1:n_perm) {
  # scramble the sex vector and then calculate difference between means
  # `sample()` with a vector as an argument yields a random permutation of the vector
  d |>
    mutate(sex = sample(sex)) |>
    summarize(diff = mean(kernel95[sex == "M"]) -
      mean(kernel95[sex == "F"])) |>
    pull(diff) -> perm_diff[[i]]
}
histogram(perm_diff)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
p <- (sum(perm_diff >= abs(obs_diff)) +
  sum(perm_diff <= -abs(obs_diff))) / n_perm
# or
p <- sum(abs(perm_diff) >= abs(obs_diff)) / n_perm
p
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## [1] 0.0011
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ladd(
  panel.abline(v = obs_diff, col = "red", lty = 3, lwd = 2)
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-2.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


We can also use the `do()*` or `replicate()` functions to do our permutations...


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# using do()*...
perm_diff <-
  {
    do(n_perm) *
      d |>
        mutate(sex = sample(sex)) |>
        summarize(diff = mean(kernel95[sex == "M"]) -
          mean(kernel95[sex == "F"]))
  } |>
  pull(diff) # extract column of value as vector
histogram(perm_diff)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# using replicate()... note the braces `{}` wrapped around the code to perform in each replicate within the `replicate()` function
perm_diff <- replicate(n_perm, {
  d |>
    mutate(sex = sample(sex)) |>
    summarize(diff = mean(kernel95[sex == "M"]) -
      mean(kernel95[sex == "F"])) |>
    pull(diff) # extract column of value as vector
})
histogram(perm_diff)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-2.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


And, again, we could do this whole process using the {infer} package workflow...


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
perm_diff <- d |>
  specify(formula = kernel95 ~ sex) |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = n_perm, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("M", "F"))

obs_diff <- d |>
  specify(formula = kernel95 ~ sex) |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("M", "F"))
obs_diff
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## Response: kernel95 (numeric)
## Explanatory: sex (factor)
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##    stat
##   <dbl>
## 1  111.
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
perm_diff |>
  get_p_value(obs_stat = obs_diff, direction = "both")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   p_value
##     <dbl>
## 1  0.0006
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
visualize(perm_diff) +
  shade_p_value(obs_stat = obs_diff, size = 0.5, fill = "#c0c0c0", direction = "both")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```

```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise-06-solution_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


  - Under this approach, what is the "null" hypothesis? What is the test statistic? Is the difference in mean kernel95 home range size "significant"?

The null hypothesis here is that the difference in mean kernel95 home range size for males versus females is zero. The test statistic is the **actual difference in mean kernel95 home range size for males versus females**, and it is evaluated relative to a permutation distribution for this statistic. Based on our very low p value (less than 0.001), under a null hypothesis significance testing framework, we would conclude that the difference is "significant" (assuming that p is less than the alpha level we specify).

#### Step 8 {.unnumbered}

- Finally, use a theory-based parametric test (e.g., a t-test) to also calculate an appropriate test statistic and associated p value for the comparison of male and female mean kernel95 home range size. Is the difference in mean kernel95 home range size "significant"?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
f <- d |> filter(sex == "F")
m <- d |> filter(sex == "M")

# first, what is ratio of variances in our two samples?
var_f <- var(f$kernel95)
var_m <- var(m$kernel95)
var_f / var_m
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## [1] 1.272656
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# ratio is less than 2.0, so we can use equal variance version of t test...

num_f <- nrow(f)
num_m <- nrow(m)

mean_f <- mean(f$kernel95)
mean_m <- mean(m$kernel95)

# hand-calculate the test statistic and p value...
s2 <- ((num_m - 1) * var_m + (num_f - 1) * var_f) / (num_m + num_f - 2)
t_stat <- (mean_m - mean_f) / sqrt(s2 * (1 / num_m + 1 / num_f))
t_stat
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## [1] 3.94816
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
df <- num_m + num_f - 2
p <- 2 * (1 - pt(t_stat, df))
p
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## [1] 0.0009426349
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# or use the t.test() function
t_test <- t.test(x = m$kernel95, y = f$kernel95, var.equal = TRUE)
t_test
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
## 
## 	Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  m$kernel95 and f$kernel95
## t = 3.9482, df = 18, p-value = 0.0009426
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##   51.91339 169.99890
## sample estimates:
## mean of x mean of y 
##  429.7407  318.7846
```


:::
:::


  - Under this approach, what is the test statistic? Is the difference in mean kernel95 home range size "significant"?

Here, the null hypothesis again is that the difference in mean kernel95 home range size for males versus females is zero. The test statistic is the actual difference in means **scaled by something equivalent to a standard error** that takes into account the variance and size of our two samples. This test statistic is then evaluated relative to a t distribution that depends on the number of degrees of freedom, which depends on the sample size of our two samples (if the variances were not roughly equal, we would calculate degrees of freedom taking those unequal variances into account). Again, based on the very low p value, we would conclude that the difference is "significant" under a null hypothesis significance testing framework (assuming that p is less than the alpha level we specify).
